body:
Two important Harappan sites in Kutch

Surkotada and Desalpar are Harappan sites in the Kutch region of Gujarat. Both are associated with substantial defensive structures, but their characteristic discoveries differ.

The presence of fortifications shows that these were organised settlements where considerable effort was devoted to constructing protective boundaries. It does not, by itself, establish the political organisation of the entire Harappan civilisation or prove that these settlements were ports.

Surkotada: a fortified citadel and residential area

Surkotada is situated in Kutch district, northeast of Bhuj and in the wider Rapar region. Excavations revealed a compact settlement with a fortified citadel and an adjoining residential area.

A citadel is a strongly built or elevated part of a settlement. At Surkotada, the citadel and residential area were protected by fortification walls constructed using materials such as mudbrick and stone rubble.

The settlement contained houses and evidence of domestic facilities, including bathrooms and drains. Finds included beads, stone blades and copper objects such as a celt and chisel. A celt is a type of axe-like tool, generally made of stone or metal.

Why Surkotada is associated with horse remains

Animal bones recovered at Surkotada have attracted particular attention. Excavation reports included bones identified as belonging to horses and asses, and some researchers interpreted part of the material as remains of the true horse.

However, the identification of the supposed horse remains has been questioned by other specialists. The distinction between closely related equids is important because remains described simply as horse bones cannot automatically be treated as universally accepted proof of domesticated horses.

The Surkotada horse identification is disputed

Secure association: Surkotada is known for its fortified Harappan settlement and animal remains that have been discussed in connection with horses.

Qualification: The identification of some remains as true domestic horse is disputed. It should not be presented as an unquestioned fact.

Desalpar (Gunthli): stone fortification and inscribed objects

Desalpar, also known as Desalpar (Gunthli), is located in the Nakhatrana area of Kutch district. Its outstanding structural feature is a massive stone fortification wall.

The fortification was constructed using substantial stone blocks. Excavation also revealed mudbrick construction within the settlement. These remains establish Desalpar as a fortified Harappan site rather than a settlement identified primarily by a dockyard.

Among its most important discoveries were 2 inscribed seals: one made of steatite and another made of copper. Excavators also reported a lettered terracotta sealing.

These are 3 distinct inscribed objects: 2 seals and 1 sealing. As explained in the study of Lothal, the seals are objects that can make impressions, whereas a sealing is an impression itself.

Other finds from Desalpar included Harappan pottery, beads and jasper weights. Taken together, the fortification and these objects confirm the settlement's Harappan affiliation.

How to distinguish the two Kutch sites

Both Surkotada and Desalpar are associated with fortifications, so the presence of a defensive wall alone may not distinguish them in an objective question.

The more useful distinction is that Surkotada is especially associated with its fortified citadel and adjoining residential area, together with the disputed horse-related finds. Desalpar is especially associated with its massive stone fortification and inscribed seals made of steatite and copper.

Neither should be confused with Lothal, whose characteristic textbook associations are a large basin, bead-making, a warehouse and trade-related remains.

Prelims focus

  • Surkotada: Kutch district, in the wider Rapar region.
  • Surkotada's structures: fortified citadel and adjoining residential area.
  • Surkotada's animal remains: horse-related identification is disputed.
  • Desalpar (Gunthli): Nakhatrana area, Kutch district.
  • Desalpar's principal finds: massive stone fortification, 2 inscribed seals and 1 lettered terracotta sealing.
  • Trap: Both sites were fortified; the disputed horse association belongs to Surkotada, not Desalpar.

[Gujarat Tourism, 'Surkotada Indus Valley Civilization', based on J. P. Joshi, Excavation at Surkotada and Exploration in Kutch, Archaeological Survey of India, 1990, pp. 14–18 and 381, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1963–64—A Review, 'Excavation at Desalpur (Gunthli), District Kutch', pp. 10–12, published 1967; Sándor Bökönyi, 'Horse Remains From the Prehistoric Site of Surkotada, Kutch, Late 3rd Millennium B.C.', South Asian Studies, vol. 13, 1997, pp. 297–307; Richard H. Meadow and Ajita K. Patel, 'A Comment on Horse Remains from Surkotada', South Asian Studies, vol. 13, 1997, pp. 308–315.]

title: Surkotada and Desalpar: Fortified Harappan Settlements of Kutch

body:
Harappan settlements in Saurashtra

The Harappan civilisation extended into the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat. Settlements such as Rangpur and Rojdi show that Harappan material traditions existed outside the major urban centres of the Indus region.

These sites are especially useful for understanding the regional spread and later continuation of Harappan culture. Their importance lies in settlement remains, pottery, ornaments and other objects rather than in a confirmed dockyard.

Rangpur: pottery traditions and later Harappan continuity

Rangpur lies in the Limbdi area of present-day Surendranagar district, near the Limbdi-Bhadar or Sukbhadar watercourse.

Excavations revealed Harappan occupation followed by changes in pottery traditions. The site is therefore associated with the study of the transition from Mature Harappan to later regional cultural phases.

Important pottery associations

Harappan pottery at Rangpur included red and buff wares, with vessel forms and painted designs related to wider Harappan traditions. Later levels showed modifications in these forms. Lustrous Red Ware, a pottery tradition characterised by its polished or shining red surface, became particularly prominent in a subsequent phase.

This sequence is significant because the end of the Mature Harappan urban period did not mean that every settlement was immediately abandoned or that all earlier craft traditions disappeared at once. Some communities continued to occupy regional settlements while modifying their pottery and other material practices.

Rangpur and Lustrous Red Ware

Rangpur is associated with a sequence of Harappan, later Harappan and subsequent pottery traditions. Lustrous Red Ware is especially characteristic of a later phase; it should not be treated as the defining pottery of all Mature Harappan cities.

Rice-related evidence at Rangpur

The published report on Rangpur described rice husks associated with mud plaster from a Harappan level. Such remains suggest that rice or rice-processing by-products were present in the region.

However, the report did not identify complete rice grains or spikelets in that sample. Therefore, this evidence should not be exaggerated into conclusive proof that extensive rice cultivation took place at Rangpur during every Harappan phase.

Rojdi: a regional Harappan settlement in Rajkot district

Rojdi, also written as Rozdi in some archaeological publications, is located in Gondal taluka of Rajkot district, near the Bhadar River.

Its settlement remains include stone foundations and evidence of a defensive wall. The site is associated with a regional Harappan tradition often described as Sorath Harappan. This term refers to a regional expression of Harappan culture in Saurashtra.

Rojdi was not simply a smaller copy of Mohenjodaro. Its remains indicate local construction practices and a settlement character different from the large planned urban centres. The classic combination of extensive brick-built streets, bathrooms and drains found at some major Harappan cities was not present in the same way at Rojdi.

Characteristic finds from Rojdi

  • Pottery: Harappan-related red wares, including bowls, jars and dishes; some vessels carried painted designs.
  • Beads: ornaments made from materials including agate, carnelian and terracotta.
  • Copper objects: excavations reported copper celts.
  • Inscribed pottery: a potsherd bearing Harappan signs has been reported.
  • Painted figure: a potsherd with a human figure holding a bow and arrow was reported from the later Harappan material.

These discoveries link Rojdi with the wider Harappan tradition while demonstrating local differences in settlement life and material culture.

Do not confuse Rangpur and Rojdi

Both sites are in Saurashtra and both have associations with Harappan pottery. The distinction begins with their locations: Rangpur is in Surendranagar district near Limbdi, while Rojdi is in Rajkot district near Gondal.

Although both are described as being near a Bhadar watercourse, the early archaeological report distinguishes the larger Bhadar River at Rojdi from the Limbdi-Bhadar near Rangpur. The similarity of the river names should not lead to the conclusion that the sites are at the same location.

For matching purposes, connect Rangpur chiefly with its pottery sequence and later Lustrous Red Ware tradition. Connect Rojdi with its Sorath Harappan character, painted pottery, beads and copper objects.

One-glance comparison of the five Gujarat sites

The five sites can be recalled through 3 geographical groups. Lothal, near the Gulf of Khambhat, is associated with a large basin, bead-making, a warehouse and seals. Surkotada and Desalpar, in Kutch, are fortified settlements distinguished respectively by disputed horse-related remains and a major stone wall with inscribed seals. Rangpur and Rojdi, in Saurashtra, preserve regional Harappan traditions distinguished respectively by a changing pottery sequence and characteristic settlement finds.

The general principle is to associate each site with its most distinctive evidence. A Harappan object such as a bead, seal or painted pot may occur at more than one site. It is the combination of location, structure and characteristic discoveries that makes a site identifiable.

Prelims focus

  • Rangpur: Limbdi area, Surendranagar district.
  • Rangpur's major association: Harappan-to-later pottery sequence, including Lustrous Red Ware in a subsequent phase.
  • Rangpur's rice evidence: husks reported; extensive cultivation is not established by that find alone.
  • Rojdi: Gondal area, Rajkot district, near the Bhadar River.
  • Rojdi's major finds: regional Harappan pottery, beads, copper celts and inscribed or painted potsherds.
  • Trap: Rangpur and Rojdi are different sites in different districts, even though both are associated with Harappan pottery.

[S. R. Rao, 'Excavation at Rangpur and Other Explorations in Gujarat', Ancient India, nos. 18–19, 1963, pp. 13–20, 60–62, 161–175 and 185–186, including the study of plant remains by S. S. Ghosh and Krishna Lal; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1993–94—A Review, 'Excavation at Rojdi, District Rajkot', p. 40, published 2000; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', pp. 1–2 and 17; Archaeological Survey of India, Ancient India, nos. 18–19, discussion of Rojdi and other Saurashtra sites, pp. 185–186.]
